newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian activist rejects Swiss court verdict.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian activist rejects Swiss court verdict.

text.p: A leading Nigerian human rights activist acquitted of theft by a Geneva criminal court on Friday rejected the verdict, saying it had not gone far enough.
"I think it is merely a collusion between the court and the police to take away the steam from the civil suit I intend to take out against them," Clement Nwankwo told Reuters in Lagos.

"I have discussed with my lawyers to file an appeal on Monday and I intend to go to the highest level of the Swiss legal system," added Nwankwo, a lawyer who heads the Constitutional Rights Project, a human rights group, in Nigeria.
The verdict of the Swiss court on Friday overturned his conviction in April that he stole two women's designer suits.
Nwankwo was in the Swiss city at the time to attend the U.N. Commission on Human Rights when he was arrested and sentenced to 20 days in jail. He denied the charges.
The ladies' suits from the boutique Anita Smaga, valued at 2,580 Swiss francs ($1,800) were never found, leading the court to rule on Friday he should be given the benefit of the doubt.

The incident embarrassed the host Swiss delegation to the annual U.N. human rights forum after Nwankwo claimed he was beaten and tortured by Geneva police. Held incommunicado in jail for four days before being swiftly sentenced, he then appealed.
"I will sue for damages for the humiliation and torture I experienced in the hands of the Swiss police," Nwankwo said.

Police, who arrested him when saleswomen reported the suits missing after he had been briefly in the chic shop, argued that physical force had been necessary to restrain him. They denied his charge that he had been beaten or handcuffed naked to a bed.
"He has been acquitted of theft but the court confirmed his conviction for resisting arrest," his lawyer, Olivier Cramer told Reuters. "It is a victory, but not a total one."
The court lifted the three-year expulsion order but kept a four-day sentence for his resisting arrest. This equalled time served in detention so there is no more time to be served.
